1.overview: Asymptotic notation answers depend on WHICH bound the question asks for. Big-Oh O(f(n)) describes an UPPER bound on growth in the WORST case — the algorithm will not do worse than f(n) for large n. Theta gives a tight bound (upper and lower), and Omega gives a lower (best-case) bound. The stem explicitly says 'worst possible set of inputs', so Big-Oh is the standard notation. Key idea (Data Structures): Big-Oh notation

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Theta notation". Theta Θ(n) means the algorithm grows proportionally to n in BOTH worst and best case — a tight bound. The question only asks for worst-case upper-bound notation, not a tight bound. Theta is stricter than what the stem requires.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Big-Oh notation". Big-Oh is the conventional notation for worst-case upper bounds in exit exams. If an algorithm's worst case is at most 3n² + 5n, we say O(n²). This directly matches 'worst possible inputs'.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Big-Omega notation". Big-Omega Ω(f(n)) describes a LOWER bound — how fast the algorithm must grow at minimum (often linked to best case). Worst-case analysis uses Big-Oh, not Omega. Picking Omega confuses best-case and worst-case notation.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "All". 'All' is never correct when the four notations serve different purposes. Only one notation specifically denotes worst-case upper bounds — Big-Oh.

1.studyTip: Worst case → Big-Oh O(·). Best case → Omega Ω(·). Tight bound → Theta Θ(·).

2.overview: Binary search repeatedly halves the search space. Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements. Halving n times until one element remains takes log₂(n) steps, giving O(log n) time. It requires a sorted array and random access (indexable structure). Key idea (Data Structures): O(log n)

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(n)". O(n) is linear search complexity — scan every element once. Binary search never examines all n elements; it eliminates half each step, which is logarithmic, not linear.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "O(n^2)". O(n²) is quadratic — typical of nested loops comparing all pairs. Binary search has one loop that divides the range, not n² work.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "O(1)". O(1) is constant time — e.g. accessing arr[0]. Binary search still performs multiple comparisons as n grows; work increases with n.
options.D: Option D (CORRECT): "O(log n)". O(log n) is correct. For n = 1,000,000, binary search needs at most about 20 comparisons (log₂ 1,000,000 ≈ 20), not millions.

2.studyTip: Sorted array + halving → binary search → O(log n).

3.overview: To find Big-O, identify the DOMINANT term — the one that grows fastest as n → ∞. Compare: log n < n < n log n < n². In T(n) = 2n + 3n² + log n + n log n + n, the term 3n² dominates because n² grows faster than every other term. Drop constants (3) and lower-order terms → O(n²). Key idea (Data Structures): O(n^2)

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(n)". O(n) would mean linear growth dominates. While 2n and n are linear terms, they are overwhelmed by 3n² for large n. Example: at n = 10,000, n = 10,000 but n² = 100,000,000 — n² wins.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "O(n^2)". O(n²) is correct. The highest-degree term is n² (coefficient 3). All other terms become insignificant compared to 3n² as n grows.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "O(log n)". O(log n) is the slowest-growing term in the entire expression (from 'log n' alone). The full function is NOT logarithmic — one small term does not define the whole complexity.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "O(n log n)". O(n log n) is faster than O(n) but slower than O(n²). Since 3n² appears in the sum, n² dominates n log n. Merge sort is O(n log n); this polynomial has an n² term, so it is quadratic, not linearithmic.

3.studyTip: List all terms → pick highest power of n → drop constants → that is Big-O.

4.overview: To insert at the END of a singly linked list when you only have a pointer to the HEAD, you must traverse from head to tail — visiting up to n nodes — then append. No tail pointer is given, so you cannot jump to the end in O(1). Traversal is O(n). With BOTH head and tail pointers, append can be O(1). Key idea (Data Structures): O(n)

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(1)". O(1) would apply only if you already had a pointer to the tail node (or a tail reference). The question states the pointer points to the HEAD only, so you must walk the whole list first.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "O(n)". O(n) is correct. In the worst case the last node is n steps from the head; each step is one pointer follow.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "O(log n)". O(log n) applies to divide-and-conquer on sorted indexable data, not linked-list traversal. Linked lists do not support random access or halving.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "O(n^2)". O(n²) would require nested loops over n — e.g. comparing every pair. A single traversal to find the tail is one pass → O(n), not O(n²).

4.studyTip: Singly linked list, head only, insert at end → traverse n nodes → O(n).

5.overview: A circular linked list is a linear list where the last node's next pointer points back to the first node, forming a ring. Singly linked ends with NULL; doubly linked has prev+next but need not wrap; a tree is hierarchical, not linear. Key idea (Data Structures): Circular linked list

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Tree". A tree is hierarchical (parent/child), not a linear list where last connects to first. Trees do not have a 'last node pointing to first' structure.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Doubly linked list". Doubly linked lists have forward and backward pointers but typically end with NULL at both ends unless explicitly made circular. The defining feature here is last→first wrap-around, which names 'circular' linked list.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Circular linked list". Circular linked list exactly matches: last node points to the first node, so traversal can continue indefinitely around the ring.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Singly linked list". Singly linked list ends with NULL at the last node — it does NOT point back to the first. That is the key difference from circular.

5.studyTip: Last → first pointer = circular linked list.
